b: Other than reclaiming Alsace-Lorraine and occupation of the Rhineland, there was no post-war occupation of Germany, certainly not in Berlin and certainly not by American forces. And the screenplay was written in 1942, so the Epsteins couldn't have been thinking of the 1945 occupation of Berlin. Presumably there were lots of WW1 veterans in the original audiences, who would have remembered *not* marching into Berlin. Is there any inspiration for this dialogue or reason it is in the film, rather than something like "I was with the Americans when they marched over the Hindenburg Line in 1918" or an actual historical event?
Edit: as pointed out by respondents, I misquoted Renault: he was with the Americans when they "blundered into Berlin" (responding to Major Strasser mocking Rick as a "blundering American")
